questions.question: A medical diagnostic test has a 95% sensitivity and 90% specificity. If a disease has a 1% prevalence in the population, what happens to the probability that a person who tests positive actually has the disease (Positive Predictive Value)?
options: It is extremely high (over 90%) because sensitivity is 95%.
It is relatively low (around 8.7%) due to the low base rate of the disease (Bayes Theorem).
It is exactly equal to the specificity (90%).
It cannot be calculated without knowing the sample size.
questions.explanation: By Bayes' Theorem, with a low prior (1%), false positives from the 99% healthy majority outnumber true positives, making the posterior probability ~8.7%.

questions.question: According to the Central Limit Theorem (CLT), which of the following statements is true regarding the sampling distribution of the sample mean?
options: The population itself must be normally distributed for CLT to hold.
The sampling distribution of the mean approaches a normal distribution as sample size n increases, regardless of the population distribution shape (given finite variance).
The standard deviation of the sample mean increases as sample size increases.
CLT applies only to discrete distributions like Poisson and Binomial.
questions.explanation: The CLT guarantees that for sufficiently large sample sizes, sample means are approximately normally distributed with standard error σ/√n.

questions.question: In hypothesis testing, what is a Type I error (α) and how does it relate to p-values?
options: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis; occurs when p-value > 0.05.
Rejecting a true null hypothesis (false positive); we reject the null when the p-value is less than the significance level α.
Incorrectly calculating the standard error of the estimate.
The probability of correctly accepting an alternative hypothesis (statistical power).
questions.explanation: A Type I error is rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true (false positive rate α).
